pass_b_english: The gifts of Zeus are not only ours, but also common to the Greeks, our relatives, and to our gentile people, for Jupiter, that is Zeus, generated Asclepius from himself.
Asclepius was sent to earth through the life-giving sun, and having made a progression from heaven to earth in human form, he appeared uniquely around Epidaurus.

From there, he extended his saving right hand to all the earth, and came to Pergamon, Ionia, Tarentum, and finally Rome, and to the island of Cos, and Agas, spreading his healing powers to all people.
He is everywhere, on land and sea, and he visits each of us, and heals the souls and bodies that are weak and afflicted.
Asclepius is considered to have been born from Zeus, appearing to the mind, but not in human form, however, he is seen in human figure, and it is said that he was born from Apollo and Coronis.

The story of his birth from Apollo and Coronis is well-known, and it is said that he was raised by a certain priest in the temple of Apollo, who was not obscure among those who were there, and who was said to have comprehended natural philosophy and medical art.
The Greeks have written many things about Asclepius, and his legend has endured for centuries, and the Egyptians have also written absurd things about him.

A certain healer, having treated the medical art and found it to be more effective than that of his predecessors, and having given it to Asclepius, who handed down the art, became arrogant and puffed up with pride, and wandered through the region, proclaiming his art and gathering riches, driven by shameful greed.
He claimed to be able to raise some from the dead, and his arrogance soon got the better of him, leading to his downfall, for he was struck by lightning, a punishment from God for his hubris.
God inflicted just punishment on him, showing that he was nothing but earth and dust, as the poet Pindar says.
Pindar says it is worthy to see what he sings about him, and that he suffers nothing, for he has earth and dust.
For God weighs human affairs with a balance in a just judgment, giving rewards or punishments according to each one's dignity, as Euripides says, and Apollo says that Zeus killed his son Asclepius.
But shall we renounce the god who has healed life through the art of medicine, simply because he has done so?

The question arises as to why the art of medicine has been so highly esteemed, and it is clear that other gods have been responsible for the development of various sciences and liberal arts, which have greatly benefited human society.

If the divine being has restored sight to the blind, given light to those who have been deprived of it, and brought the dead back to life, and if he has ordered the lame to walk and the straight to return home, what can he possibly gain from us that would lead us to suspect him?
When individuals are cured of certain ailments, they are, in a sense, reborn into a new life, and they praise the doctor, and he is to be praised for his medical skill.

The most skilled physician, having acquired a deep understanding of the human condition through his medical experience, has elevated avarice and pride to an undeserved pedestal, and he praises himself.
The Hebrews, too, have been known to boast of the gifts they have received from God, and you have defected from our community.
